title: Twenty-Four Hours or Twenty-Four Months: It’s Time for Peace in Ukraine | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Michael Froman assesses the Abu Dhabi talks as useful (direct talks, restored mil-to-mil contact, prisoner exchange) but short of a ceasefire nearly five years into the war; Ukraine has shown flexibility on territory and NATO, while Putin remains maximalist despite huge costs. With Europe now admitted to the next round and Congress post-midterms a possible pressure point, he argues the key is changing Putin's cost/benefit calculus, which only Trump can potentially deliver.

themes.theme: Abu Dhabi outcomes and the negotiating agenda

insights.claim: The Abu Dhabi trilateral talks restored direct discussions and military-to-military talks, including the presence of U.S. EUCOM commander and NATO SACEUR General Alexus Grynkewich, and produced a prisoner-exchange agreement but no ceasefire.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Restored mil-to-mil channels lower escalation risk, but absence of ceasefire keeps war-risk premia in place.
insights.locator: It wasn’t a joke, but the talks

insights.claim: The Ukraine negotiating agenda has relatively few issues—territorial control/recognition, security guarantees/associations, economic autonomy, political independence—but they are existential in nature, making compromise hard.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Small agenda but existential stakes means binary, headline-driven outcomes rather than gradual progress.

insights.claim: After Abu Dhabi, Kushner and Witkoff met Putin in Moscow and then Zelenskyy in Dublin, without a breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Continued shuttle diplomacy keeps peace optionality alive into winter.
insights.quote: No puffs of white smoke yet
insights.locator: The trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi

themes.theme: Asymmetric flexibility: Ukraine bends, Putin does not

insights.claim: Some Ukrainians quietly argue there is nothing sacrosanct about pre-2022 or pre-2014 borders, signaling openness to options on territory, though not to ceding unconquered land or legally recognizing dismemberment.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: De facto (not de jure) territorial arrangements are the likely shape of any deal.
insights.quote: there is nothing sacrosanct about the pre-2022 borders, let alone the pre-2014 ones
insights.locator: Ukrainians have been eager to bring

insights.claim: Ukraine has shown flexibility by no longer insisting on NATO membership, seeking instead meaningful, credible security guarantees to deter another Russian war.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: The design of security guarantees, not NATO accession, is now the core variable for a settlement.
insights.quote: no longer insisting on NATO membership, just meaningful, credible security guarantees
insights.locator: Ukrainians have been eager to bring

insights.claim: Putin appears not to have moved off maximalist demands even though the war has outlasted World War I, Russia has suffered over a million casualties, and Russia has gained only about 12 percent of Ukraine's territory since February 2022.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Russian intransigence remains the binding constraint; battlefield costs have not yet translated into concessions.
insights.quote: Russia has suffered more than a million casualties
insights.locator: Russian President Vladimir Putin, on the other hand

insights.claim: Ukrainian drones have knocked nearly a third of Russia's refining capacity offline.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Strikes on Russian refining affect fuel product exports and refined-product margins; a ceasefire could restore that capacity.
insights.quote: Ukrainian drones have knocked nearly a third of its refining capacity offline
insights.locator: Russian President Vladimir Putin, on the other hand

insights.claim: Winter promises to be brutal for Ukrainians whose energy infrastructure and cities are attacked nightly, and both sides are seeking battlefield advantage to maximize negotiating leverage.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Expect escalating energy-infrastructure strikes near-term as leverage-building before any deal.
insights.quote: Both sides are trying to gain advantage on the battlefield to maximize whatever leverage

themes.theme: U.S. domestic politics as a lever

insights.claim: After the midterm elections, the new Congress may pressure the Trump administration to support Ukraine more; while it can hardly force arms shipments, it retains power of the purse and could push intelligence sharing and Starlink availability for Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Watch bipartisan appropriations and Starlink/intelligence provisions as signals of U.S. support durability.
insights.quote: Congress does retain the power of the purse
insights.locator: This is happening in the context

insights.claim: Froman concludes the key is changing Putin's cost/benefit analysis through sticks and carrots, and that only President Trump is potentially capable of delivering him, if he chooses to.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Settlement odds hinge on Trump's willingness to apply pressure/incentives on Russia (e.g., sanctions); track his posture.
insights.quote: the only party potentially capable of delivering him is President Trump, if he chooses to do so

themes.theme: Europe's seat at the table and security architecture

insights.claim: European nations were not directly in the Abu Dhabi three-party talks but were 'in the next room'; Froman argues their defense spending push toward 5 percent of GDP and aid to Ukraine have earned them a seat.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Europe's 5%-of-GDP defense commitment underpins a multi-year defense spending cycle regardless of peace.
insights.quote: as they raise European spending on defense toward their 5 percent of GDP commitment
insights.locator: Abroad, Europe has been working hard

insights.claim: Witkoff announced that Russia had agreed to let Europe participate in the next round of negotiations, which Froman sees as a positive step and possibly a sign of the Trump administration valuing allies.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: European inclusion improves implementability of any agreement involving sanctions and guarantees.
insights.locator: Abroad, Europe has been working hard

insights.claim: Trump's mention that European security architecture was on the Abu Dhabi agenda sparked European fears of a U.S. NATO drawdown or concessions to Putin's demand to pull NATO back from Russia's borders.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: U.S. commitment to NATO remains a tail risk driving European defense autonomy spending.
insights.locator: On the eve of Abu Dhabi

insights.claim: Kushner laid out five pillars for European security—permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal de-escalation measures, and an enduring long-term framework—which Froman likens to Cold War-era NATO and OSCE practices.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
entities: Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe
insights.so_what: The proposed architecture resembles Cold War confidence-building, implying managed rivalry rather than normalization.
insights.quote: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal de-escalation measures
insights.locator: On the eve of Abu Dhabi

insights.claim: Froman judges the situation 'ripe for progress' given Ukrainian flexibility and European inclusion, noting the conflict was never going to be resolved in twenty-four hours and 'we're coming up on twenty-four months'.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Author leans toward a near-term settlement window; a ceasefire would reprice European risk assets and energy.
insights.quote: The situation seems ripe for progress.
